plot_extraction.response_text:
When carpet tackers hired to prepare the State Capitol for Prince Ludwig’s visit form a union overnight and strike for double pay, the Governor refuses to be pressured. Unable to hire replacements, state officials, legislators, judges, and other prominent citizens unite to lay the carpets themselves, setting aside political rivalries and working enthusiastically to finish before the Prince’s scheduled arrival.

Meanwhile, a U.S. senator secretly arranges for the Prince to arrive early, believing he should witness Americans as they truly are rather than through formal ceremonies. Hidden above the rotunda, the Prince watches the disheveled dignitaries cooperate, mend disputes, and perform manual labor. When discovered, he joins them and enjoys the spontaneous scene more than any staged reception, concluding that the best way to see America is when America does not know it is being observed.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a brisk, genial mode of social comedy, combining journalistic clarity with affectionate political satire. Its premise is mildly farcical—a newly formed carpet-tackers’ union halts urgent work just before a royal visit—but the narration treats the escalating absurdity with enough seriousness to make the comedy feel plausible. The dominant tone is amused, buoyant and civic-minded rather than caustic. Politicians, officials, labourers and dignitaries are teased for their pride and self-importance, yet the story remains broadly sympathetic to them. Even conflict becomes an opportunity to celebrate initiative, fellowship and an informal national character.

The narration is third-person and largely omniscient, moving freely among public scenes, private schemes and individual reactions. The narrator generally remains outside the characters but occasionally steps forward with knowing commentary, as in the playful correction that there were “good, bad and—no, there were no indifferent,” or the observation that “There should have been a Boswell there.” Such interventions give the voice the character of an entertaining raconteur: socially observant, lightly ironic and confident that the reader shares its amusement. The perspective is panoramic, well suited to a story about collective action. Rather than following one central protagonist throughout, it passes among the Governor, Harry Weston, Senator Bruner, the carpet-tackers and Prince Ludwig, allowing the State-house itself to function as the story’s communal centre.

The prose alternates between efficient exposition and dialogue-heavy dramatic scenes. Narrative sentences often gather detail through parallel clauses and cumulative lists: work stops “in the Senate Chamber and in the House, on the stairways and in the corridors,” while later the action embraces Republicans and Democrats, friends and enemies, senators, judges, bankers and union leaders. This repeated use of enumeration creates bustle, enlarges the scale of the episode and reinforces the theme of disparate people being drawn into common activity. Short declarative sentences punctuate these longer constructions—“There was magic in its note”; “That settled it”; “It went without a hitch”—giving the narrative a confident, anecdotal rhythm. Exclamation marks, dashes, parenthetical interruptions and repeated words reproduce excitement and spontaneous speech. The onomatopoeic “Stretch—stretch—stretch, and tack—tack—tack” briefly converts the work itself into a comic refrain.

Dialogue is the principal means of characterisation. It is colloquial, quick and strongly marked by early twentieth-century American idiom: “pretty bum,” “hummer,” “tickled,” “got next to the situation,” “jolly up,” “the boys,” and “sure-enough thing.” Grammatical informality—“We was anxious,” “What’s the matter with us?”—distinguishes working-class and conversational voices without making them opaque. Public figures speak in a mixture of political rhetoric and everyday slang, and much of the humour comes from applying grand oratory to carpet-laying. Harry Weston transforms manual work into a patriotic campaign; Senator Arnold speaks of driving tacks as another form of service to the State; and the Governor issues solemn pronouncements about carpets, collars and the potentially distracting “feminine element.” The gap between elevated language and mundane activity supplies the story’s characteristic comic incongruity.

Characterisation is economical and behavioural. Figures are established through a revealing phrase, gesture or manner of speaking rather than through sustained psychological analysis. The Governor is energetic, proud and resistant to coercion; Weston is charismatic and tactically shrewd; Bruner is mischievous but frames his mischief as patriotic duty; the Prince is distinguished chiefly by his relief at escaping ceremony. Minor characters are similarly vivid in miniature: the striker takes courage from the floor’s splinters, the elderly senator tests his muscle, and Bridget Haggerty dispenses coffee, sandwiches and loud moral judgment. Many characters are identified by office rather than by name, making them simultaneously individuals and representatives of political or civic types.

The plot is tightly organised around a deadline. The opening gives exact times, the Prince is expected at four, and later references to noon, two o’clock and the approaching finish sustain momentum. The structure proceeds through clean stages: stoppage, explanation, failed attempts to hire replacements, collective improvisation, the secret acceleration of the Prince’s arrival, covert observation and final revelation. Each development raises the comic stakes. The first reversal turns lawmakers into carpet-tackers; the second allows the royal visitor to see them before they can restore their formal appearance. Suspense depends not on danger but on timing, concealment and the possibility of dignified people being caught undignified.

The humour is warm, cumulative and situational. It draws on reversals of status, political rivalries temporarily suspended, exaggerated solemnity and the collision between ceremonial expectations and physical labour. The story repeatedly places prestigious men in undignified postures: dirty, collarless, nursing bruised fingers, arguing over hammers or collaborating with old enemies on wrinkles in a carpet. Running jokes about official rivalry, legislative competition, labour politics and public dignity deepen the comic texture. Hyperbole—“millennium-like unity,” “worked like a Trojan,” “Indian traditions to burn”—keeps the narrative lively while preserving its newspaper-anecdote accessibility.

The setting is rendered primarily as a social arena rather than through lyrical description. The State-house’s chambers, offices, corridors, stairways, rotunda, tunnel and storerooms create a theatrical architecture in which public roles can be rearranged. Before the work, the bare boards are splintered and “miserable”; afterward, the building is restored through communal effort. The contrast between the formal Capitol and its improvised backstage areas supports the central opposition between official display and unguarded reality. The hidden vantage point above the rotunda is especially important: it turns the Prince into a spectator watching authentic national life as though it were a play.

The thematic emphasis falls on democratic informality, self-reliance and authenticity. The story idealises an America revealed not by bands, speeches, uniforms or polished receptions, but by people abandoning rank and working together. It does not offer a complex treatment of labour conflict: the strike is largely framed as an opportunistic “hold-up,” and the officials’ amateur labour becomes the more celebrated form of solidarity. Nevertheless, the union figures are not portrayed as villains of great menace; they belong to the same comic civic world, and even the teamsters’ union president eventually joins the effort. Political antagonisms likewise prove superficial when practical action is required.

The ending condenses the story’s governing idea into an epigram: “the only way to see America is to see it when America is not seeing you.” This polished final line resolves the farce while converting it into a statement about national identity. It also crystallises the story’s stylistic method. Throughout, public ceremony is displaced by backstage observation, formal rhetoric by slang, and political dignity by physical comedy. The resulting style is energetic, conversational and theatrically constructed, with a strong period flavour and an optimistic belief that character is most truthfully displayed through spontaneous action rather than prepared spectacle.

## THE ROYAL CARPET

At nine o’clock on Thursday morning there were forty-two carpet-tackers at work in the State Capitol.

At nine-fifteen there were none.

The transformation occurred without noise, violence, or even undue haste. One man ceased tapping in the Senate Chamber; two more straightened themselves painfully in the House; six abandoned the east corridor; and the remainder came in from stairways, committee rooms, reception rooms and remote official apartments, carrying their hammers with the solemnity of soldiers stacking arms.

They assembled under the rotunda.

Mr. Silas Crump, who had been a carpet-tacker for eighteen years and a labour leader since breakfast, mounted a roll of crimson Wilton.

“Boys,” he said, “we are now Local Number One of the United Carpet-Fitters, Stretchers, Layers and Tackers of this State.”

The boys applauded.

“Furthermore,” said Mr. Crump, “we got rights.”

They applauded the rights.

“Furthermore, we want double pay from this minute until the royal feet has passed over the last yard.”

That was applauded most of all.

Five minutes later a delegation waited upon Amos Peacock, Superintendent of Public Buildings, who had not yet heard of the union and had never suspected that carpet-tackers possessed a collective soul.

“Double pay!” cried Peacock. “Why?”

“Emergency work,” said Crump.

“You knew it was emergency work when you took it.”

“We didn’t have no organization then.”

“You didn’t have one twenty minutes ago.”

“We got one now.”

Mr. Crump said it quietly. He had taken courage from the naked floor. It was an astonishingly bad floor—splintered, stained, scarred by generations of desks, boots, cuspidors and public questions. To leave that floor uncovered for Prince Ludwig of Hohenwald was to expose the Commonwealth in its stockings.

The Prince was due at four.

Superintendent Peacock looked at the floor, looked at the clocks, looked at Mr. Crump, and went to the Governor.

Governor Temple was dictating a proclamation on Forestry Week. He was a large, square gentleman with a fighting chin and a collar which made surrender physiologically difficult.

“They have done what?” he demanded.

“Organized, sir.”

“Overnight?”

“Since nine o’clock.”

“And they want double wages?”

“Until the Prince has walked over the carpets.”

The Governor removed his spectacles.

“Peacock, no man may hold up this State by sitting on its Brussels.”

“They aren’t sitting on it, Governor. They are standing around it.”

“Same principle. Tell them no.”

Peacock went out, returned, and said, “They say very well.”

“What do they mean by that?”

“They mean they will not work.”

The Governor’s chin advanced.

“Hire others.”

“We have telephoned every firm in the city. Crump’s men got to them first.”

“Bring men from outside.”

“The train would not get them here before three-ten.”

“Then use floor cloth.”

“There isn’t enough.”

“Paint the boards.”

“It would not dry.”

For the first time the Governor looked troubled. He walked to a window and saw the reviewing stand below, the flags along the avenue, the cavalry horses being rubbed to an official brilliance, and the bandmaster conducting an imaginary march with both arms. Everything was ready for royalty except the floors.

“Double wages!” said the Governor. “It is blackmail with a tack hammer.”

Secretary of State Wilbur Ames, who had entered during the crisis, coughed discreetly.

“Governor, could we not—merely as a practical matter—”

“No.”

“But the Prince—”

“If Prince Ludwig cannot admire a free people on bare boards, he is no democrat.”

“I believe he is a prince,” said Ames.

“All the more reason to educate him.”

Yet the Governor knew that the State could not educate a prince by inviting him to trip over carpet rolls. He called a conference for ten o’clock.

It was a distinguished conference. The Attorney-General came, and the Treasurer, and the Speaker of the House, and the President of the Senate. Chief Justice Bell arrived in robes because he had been interrupted in court. Senator Arnold came because he went everywhere. Harry Weston came because everybody sent for Harry when something impossible had to be made popular.

Weston was young for a political manager and cheerful for any kind of manager. He had an engaging grin, an inexhaustible supply of fresh collars, and the dangerous habit of making other men believe that his ideas had originally been theirs.

The situation was explained.

“Pretty tight,” he observed.

“Outrageous,” said the Attorney-General.

“Unconstitutional,” said the Treasurer.

“Against public policy,” said the Chief Justice.

“Can we arrest them?” asked the Speaker.

“For what?” said the Attorney-General.

“For being carpet-tackers at a time like this.”

“No statute covers it.”

“Then what good,” demanded the Speaker, “is the legislature?”

This question had often been asked, but never by the Speaker.

Weston strolled to the Senate Chamber. The others followed. Rolls of green carpet lay about like fallen columns. The floor stretched broad, bare and humiliating before them.

“How many men does it take?” Weston asked.

“Forty,” said Peacock.

“How long?”

“Professionals might finish by half-past three.”

“Could eighty amateurs do it by the same time?”

“They might ruin the carpet.”

“Could they cover the floor?”

“In a manner of speaking.”

“Then,” said Weston, “let us speak in that manner.”

The Governor stared at him.

“You propose that we lay it ourselves?”

“I propose that the State government go to the floor for the honour of the State.”

Senator Arnold bent down, picked up a tack hammer, tested its balance and struck a tack into a convenient crack. The tack went in. So did a portion of the Senator’s thumb.

He rose with dignity.

“There is nothing,” he said, concealing the thumb behind his back, “inconsistent between statesmanship and skilled labour.”

That decided it.

Messengers ran through the Capitol. Telephones rang. Committee hearings stopped in the middle of testimony. The House adjourned while Representative Dooley was speaking, an event which six previous Speakers had attempted without success. Judges postponed decisions, commissioners abandoned statistics, clerks came out of their offices, and prominent citizens were summoned from banks, clubs, law firms and luncheon counters.

The call was simple:

THE CAPITOL MUST BE CARPETED BY FOUR. BRING A HAMMER.

There was magic in it.

At ten-thirty the State-house resembled a workshop which had unexpectedly elected itself. Republicans and Democrats, reformers and regulars, wet men and dry men, corporation lawyers and enemies of corporations swarmed through the chambers. Some brought hammers; some brought enthusiasm; a few brought advice. The advice was plentiful and, as usual, hardest to use.

Harry Weston stood on the clerk’s desk in the House.

“Gentlemen,” he cried, “this is no time for party lines!”

Representative Mulrooney looked at the carpet.

“It’s full of lines,” he objected.

“Those are to be matched,” said Weston. “Party lines are to be forgotten.”

He divided them into squads. The Senate took its own chamber, on the theory that its members understood its irregularities. The House tackled the larger room, maintaining that anything the Senate could do slowly the House could do loudly. Judges were assigned to the Supreme Court rooms; department heads to the corridors; bankers to the grand staircase, because they were accustomed to high places; and newspaper men nowhere at all, because they refused to work while there was anything to report.

The first fifteen minutes were chiefly constitutional debate.

“Do we stretch north and south?”

“East and west.”

“Why?”

“Precedent.”

“What precedent?”

“Every carpet I ever saw.”

“That is custom, not precedent.”

The Chief Justice settled the point by ordering both sides to pull. The carpet stretched diagonally.

After that they learned.

Coats came off. Collars wilted. Suspenders appeared in public life. Men who had not knelt since childhood dropped to their knees and discovered that the human body contains joints which political office does not exercise. The air filled with taps, thumps, grunts and exhortations.

“Hold her!”

“I am holding her!”

“Not you—the carpet!”

“Who took my hammer?”

“You were using mine.”

“I deny it.”

“You’ve got my initials on the handle.”

“Then your initials have been using my hand.”

Stretch—pull—flatten—and tack, tack, tack!

Governor Temple moved through the building like a field commander. He had tied a white handkerchief around his collar, removed his coat, and acquired a long scratch across his left cheek.

“No wrinkles!” he ordered. “This administration will not be judged by wrinkles.”

“What about the west corridor?” Peacock asked.

“Put the opposition there.”

“Why?”

“They are experienced in smoothing things over.”

At eleven o’clock the union delegation returned to see how surrender was progressing.

It was not progressing.

Mr. Crump stood in the doorway of the House and watched the Lieutenant-Governor crawl backward under a desk while three legislators bounced on a stubborn rise in the carpet. The dignity of the scene impressed him less than its noise.

“You fellows are spoiling good goods,” he said.

The Lieutenant-Governor emerged, dusty but triumphant.

“They belong to the State.”

“And you ain’t laying them right.”

“They belong to the State when laid wrong, too.”

Crump examined the edge professionally.

“You’ll never make four o’clock.”

“Then,” said the Lieutenant-Governor, “we shall abolish four o’clock.”

Crump withdrew to consult his men.

The strikers had expected a darkened Capitol, terrified officials and a Governor begging for terms. Instead, they found a festival. More volunteers arrived every minute. Old political enemies shook the same carpet. Men who had not spoken for ten years shouted intimate insults at one another and enjoyed it. The President of the Teamsters’ Union, who came to inspect the labour controversy, was handed a hammer by Harry Weston and put in charge of six bank directors before he could escape.

“Now, see here,” he protested, “I’m union.”

“So are they,” said Weston. “Union of bank directors.”

“A bank director ain’t labour.”

“He will be in five minutes.”

The teamster president looked at the directors. They looked helpless. His face softened.

“You boys ever drive a tack?”

One of them admitted that he had once driven a nail into a packing case.

“Lord!” said the teamster president. “All right. Watch me.”

By noon he was the most energetic man in the north corridor.

At twelve-fifteen Bridget Haggerty took command of refreshments. Bridget supervised the Capitol cleaning women, six nieces, two aldermen and her husband, though Mr. Haggerty did not know it. She established coffee urns beneath the rotunda and sent baskets of sandwiches into every room.

“Eat!” she cried. “You can’t save a State on an empty stomach, though many of you have tried governing one with an empty head.”

No one resented Bridget. A Chief Justice may rebuke an attorney, a Governor may dismiss a commissioner, but only a woman with hot coffee can tell an entire government the truth and receive thanks for it.

While all this was occurring, Senator Felix Bruner was engaged in an enterprise of his own.

Bruner was a United States senator, a patriot, a practical joker and a man who considered secrecy wasted unless it led to a revelation. He had been placed in charge of receiving Prince Ludwig at the railway station at four o’clock. At eleven he telephoned Colonel Voss, the Prince’s military secretary, who had arrived with the royal party at a country estate twenty miles away.

“Colonel,” he said, “does His Highness truly wish to understand America?”

“That is his profound desire.”

“Then bring him in at two.”

“But the ceremony is at four.”

“Exactly.”

“I do not comprehend.”

“The ceremony is what we want him to see. Two o’clock is what we are.”

There was a pause.

“Is this proper?” asked Colonel Voss.

“No,” said Bruner. “That is why it will be valuable.”

The arrangement was made. The Prince’s motorcar would enter through the service gate. Bruner would meet him at the old tunnel beneath the east wing and conduct him unseen to the gallery above the rotunda.

Senator Bruner then joined the carpet-layers and said nothing.

At one o’clock the Capitol had passed from confusion to efficiency. Hands had blistered, tempers had warmed, and skill had appeared. The Secretary of Agriculture could judge a straight seam at twenty feet. A former Governor developed genius with a stretcher. The minority leader, who had opposed every measure introduced by the majority leader for twelve years, discovered that the two of them could fit a corner only by trusting each other.

“Pull when I say,” said the majority leader.

“You always say that.”

“This isn’t a bill. Pull!”

They pulled. The corner fitted.

The two men sat back and regarded it.

“We’ve been fools,” said the minority leader.

“About what?”

“This corner.”

“Oh,” said the majority leader.

Reconciliation has its limits.

In the Senate Chamber the elderly Senator Arnold worked beside young Representative Pike, who hoped to defeat him at the next election. Arnold’s knees ached; Pike’s hammering was violent and inaccurate.

“Young man,” said Arnold, “you strike as you speak.”

“How is that?”

“Often, hard and not quite on the point.”

Pike laughed.

“And you hold the tack as you hold office, Senator.”

“How is that?”

“Longer than anybody expects.”

The Senator considered this. Then he laughed too. Ten minutes later he showed Pike how to angle a tack beneath the baseboard, and Pike, who had never taken advice from him in public, took it gladly on the floor.

There should have been a historian present. There were reporters, of course, but reporters were occupied with the scratches, the torn trousers and the Attorney-General’s collision with a paste bucket. A historian might have noted the greater marvel: men changed positions without changing principles, accepted orders without demanding patronage, and performed useful labour without appointing an investigating commission.

At one-forty-five Senator Bruner slipped away.

He met the royal motorcar at the service gate. Prince Ludwig stepped out wearing a plain grey coat and an expression of intense relief. He was a tall, fair young man with a trained moustache and tired eyes.

“No band?” he asked.

“Not yet.”

“No schoolchildren?”

“They believe you are twenty miles away.”

“No address of welcome?”

“I have it in my pocket.”

The Prince glanced at Colonel Voss.

“Senator, I like your country already.”

They entered through the tunnel, climbed a narrow iron stair and reached the circular gallery above the rotunda. A dusty curtain concealed them. Through a slit they could look down upon the great central floor.

The Prince looked.

Below him, the government of the State was eating sandwiches on carpet rolls.

Governors, senators, judges, mayors, clerks, labour leaders, millionaires and janitors sat in friendly disorder. Some were black with dust; some had bandaged fingers; one eminent jurist had a streak of paste in his hair. Bridget Haggerty moved among them with coffee. The Governor stood on an upturned bucket, speaking.

“Fellow workers,” he said, “we have two hours left.”

“Less eating, more tacking!” shouted someone.

“That is the substance of my remarks,” said the Governor.

They rose with a cheer.

The Prince leaned forward.

“Is this prepared for me?”

“The carpets are,” whispered Bruner. “The rest is an accident.”

“Who are those two men?”

“Political enemies.”

“They are carrying the same roll.”

“Tomorrow they may deny it.”

“And that gentleman without his collar?”

“The Governor.”

“The Governor?”

“He mislaid his dignity in the House Chamber. It may be under a desk.”

Prince Ludwig smiled. Then he laughed. It was the first unroyal laugh he had enjoyed in three weeks.

From their hidden gallery they watched the work recommence. The building rang again.

Pull—stretch—steady—and tap, tap, tap!

A judge crawled beneath a radiator. A corporation president held tacks in his mouth while an anti-corporation senator hammered. The teamsters’ leader scolded six bankers for loafing. Mr. Crump and three of the striking carpet-tackers stood at the edge of the rotunda, wearing the uncertain expressions of men whose grievance had become a community picnic without them.

Crump watched the Attorney-General struggle with a seam.

“That’s upside down,” he said at last.

The Attorney-General looked up.

“Which?”

“The strip. The nap runs the other way.”

“We meant it so.”

“You did not.”

“No,” admitted the Attorney-General. “We did not.”

Crump removed his coat.

“Gimme that stretcher.”

The other strikers stared.

“What about the union?” one asked.

“The union can keep its principles,” said Crump. “I’m saving the carpet.”

He dropped to his knees. In another moment all four were at work. No agreement was signed, no wage scale conceded, no victory announced. They simply could not endure bad craftsmanship.

The Prince nudged Bruner.

“The strikers have joined?”

“Temporarily.”

“Who won?”

Bruner considered.

“The floor, I reckon.”

At two-thirty the Senate Chamber was done. The Senate marched into the House to offer assistance and criticism. The House rejected the criticism but accepted the assistance. At three the corridors were complete. Only the rotunda remained, and there the great circular carpet had to be fitted around pillars, registers and the marble base of the statue of General Arbuthnot.

General Arbuthnot had stood in bronze for sixty years with one arm extended toward the west. No one knew why. Now his gesture seemed to say, “Pull it that way.”

They did.

The Prince had watched for more than an hour. His cheeks were flushed, and every time he saw a hammer idle he shifted impatiently.

“Senator,” he whispered, “there are wrinkles near that pillar.”

“His Highness has an eye.”

“They are pulling unevenly.”

“Amateurs.”

“I have laid carpet.”

Bruner turned.

“You?”

“During military service. Our colonel believed officers should know everything soldiers did.”

Below, Harry Weston called for six more men.

The Prince took off his coat.

“Your Highness!” breathed Colonel Voss.

“I cannot watch incompetence in silence.”

“You will be seen.”

“That,” said the Prince, “has been the object of my journey.”

Before either man could stop him, he came through the curtain, descended the narrow stair and stepped from a small door behind the statue.

For several seconds no one noticed him. Royalty, without decorations, is at a disadvantage in a crowd of shirt sleeves.

He went directly to the wrinkled carpet.

“Not so hard on the left,” he said. “You must ease it around the pillar.”

Senator Arnold handed him a stretcher.

“Then ease it.”

The Prince knelt and did so. He worked expertly.

“Where’d you learn that?” asked Representative Pike.

“In the army.”

“Regular?”

“For a time.”

“You with the visiting party?”

“Yes.”

“Foreign, ain’t you?”

“Yes.”

“Well, you got sense. Hold that edge.”

The Prince held it.

Colonel Voss appeared behind the statue looking as though monarchy had fallen down the stairs. Senator Bruner followed, enjoying himself indecently.

The Prince hammered three tacks. Then Governor Temple came across the rotunda, wiping his face.

“Weston, who’s the new man?”

Weston looked. His mouth opened.

The Governor looked again.

His hand went instinctively to his collar and found none.

“Your—Your Highness!”

Every hammer stopped.

Silence moved outward in circles. The Attorney-General removed two tacks from his mouth. The teamster president stood at attention. Bridget Haggerty, who had never met a prince, curtsied to the paste bucket and recovered quickly.

Prince Ludwig remained on one knee, holding the stretcher.

“I beg you,” he said, “do not stop. This wrinkle is almost conquered.”

Nobody moved.

The Governor attempted to remember his welcoming address. What he remembered was the paragraph comparing the State’s mountains to the everlasting friendship of nations. There were no mountains at hand, only a prince on the carpet and a hundred citizens looking as if they had been shaken out of a laundry bag.

“Your Highness,” he began, “the people of this Commonwealth—”

“Are doing excellent work,” said the Prince.

The Governor looked around.

They were. The bare, miserable boards had vanished beneath deep colours. The chambers and corridors had been transformed. His people, however, had not been improved ceremonially. The Speaker’s sleeve was torn. The Chief Justice’s knees were grey. Harry Weston had lost his fresh collar at last.

“We had expected,” said the Governor, “to receive you under somewhat different conditions.”

“So had I,” said the Prince. “I am glad we were both disappointed.”

That rescued everybody.

Someone laughed. Someone else applauded. Then the rotunda burst into cheers—not the measured cheers of a reception committee, but a loud, ragged, hammer-waving roar.

Prince Ludwig rose and bowed. Bridget Haggerty pushed through the crowd and handed him coffee.

“It’s been standing,” she said, “but princes can’t expect everything.”

He drank it.

“Madam, it is magnificent.”

“It is not. But you’re civil.”

The Governor regained command.

“Gentlemen—and Bridget—we still have forty minutes.”

“Thirty-eight,” called Superintendent Peacock.

“Then to work!”

They went back to it, now with royalty in the centre squad. Prince Ludwig stretched; the Governor held; Crump directed; Senator Arnold hammered; Pike supplied tacks; and Bruner sat on the base of General Arbuthnot’s statue offering advice until Bridget ordered him down to work.

At three-forty-seven the last tack went in.

At three-fifty the workers stood in the completed rotunda and surveyed their achievement. It was not perfect. There was a doubtful seam near the east arch, a slight bulge outside the Treasurer’s office, and one strip in the House which Crump said would haunt him to his grave. But it was down, it was handsome, and it belonged unmistakably to them.

At four o’clock the band outside began the royal march.

The official car, empty except for Colonel Voss’s hat, approached the main entrance according to schedule. The reception committee lined up hastily. Coats had been brushed, faces washed and collars borrowed, though several prominent men still carried bandaged thumbs.

Prince Ludwig insisted upon entering by the front door with the rest of them.

The speeches were shortened. The parade was shortened. The formal banquet that evening was not shortened, because formal banquets cannot be, but the Prince endured it cheerfully. Whenever an orator praised international fellowship, he looked down the table at the Governor’s bruised finger, Crump’s clean collar, Bruner’s secret smile and Bridget Haggerty, who had somehow been invited and was telling the ambassador to eat his potatoes.

Near midnight Senator Bruner asked the Prince what had most impressed him in America—the Capitol, the cavalry, the factories, the schools, the speeches or the banquet.

The Prince considered.

“I think,” he said, “a nation is most interesting before it has time to pose.”

Then he glanced toward the long corridor, where two old political enemies were on their knees pressing down a seam that had risen during dinner.

“And perhaps,” he added, “the best view of a free country is obtained when it does not know anyone is looking.”

The Last Lighthouse Keeper

On the morning the sea returned the bottle, Mara Vale was repairing the lighthouse clock.

The clock had not told the correct time in twenty-three years, but it still rang every hour with such confidence that no one on the island dared correct it. Its bell was louder than the chapel’s, louder than the foghorn, and almost as loud as Mara’s father had been when he laughed.

At nine—or what the clock believed was nine—Mara stood on a ladder beneath its brass face, tightening a screw while rain whispered against the lantern-room windows. Far below, waves broke over the black rocks of Bellweather Island.

The bottle arrived on the tide.

Mara did not see it. She heard about it from Tom Tern, the baker’s son, who climbed the lighthouse steps two at a time and burst into the lantern room with his hair pasted flat by rain.

“Mara,” he gasped, bending over with both hands on his knees. “There’s a bottle.”

“There are many bottles.”

“Not like this one.”

“Green?”

“Blue.”

“That changes everything.”

“It has your name in it.”

Mara stopped turning the screwdriver.

Tom straightened and held out his hand. In it lay a small glass bottle, dark blue and sealed with white wax. Something pale was rolled inside.

“Where did you find it?”

“On Widow’s Beach. Wedged between the ribs of the old wreck.”

“No one goes to Widow’s Beach in this weather.”

“I do.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “But no one sensible.”

She climbed down from the ladder and took the bottle. The glass was cold enough to hurt her fingers. Her name had been written on the paper inside in a narrow, slanted hand.

Mara Vale.

She knew that handwriting.

For a moment, the sea disappeared. The rain disappeared. The lighthouse, with its iron stairs and soot-stained walls, seemed to tilt around her.

“Mara?” Tom asked.

She carried the bottle to the workbench beneath the great lamp. With a knife, she cut through the wax. The cork came loose with a soft sigh, as if the bottle had been holding its breath.

The note inside was dry.

Mara,

If the sea gives you this letter, then the light has gone out.

Do not trust what returns with the fog.

Ring the bell before midnight.

I am sorry.

Father

Mara read it twice.

Then she turned the page over.

Nothing.

Tom leaned closer. “Is it from him?”

“Yes.”

“But your father—”

“I know.”

Elias Vale had been dead for seven years.

Everyone on Bellweather knew the story. On a winter night, while a storm split fishing boats from their anchors, the lighthouse lamp had failed. Elias had climbed outside to repair the mechanism. Mara, fifteen years old and terrified, had waited below with a coil of rope.

The lamp came back.

Elias did not.

In the morning, they found one glove caught on an iron rail. His body was never recovered.

For seven years, Mara had kept the lighthouse in his place.

Tom glanced toward the lamp, which burned steadily behind its thick crystal lens. “The light hasn’t gone out.”

“Not yet.”

The lighthouse clock rang once.

Tom looked up. “Isn’t it morning?”

“According to the clock, it’s one.”

“That seems bad.”

“It’s always bad.”

Outside, fog crawled across the water.

It came from the north, thick and low, moving against the wind.

Mara folded the letter and slipped it into her pocket. “Go home.”

Tom stared at her. “You can’t say something like that after a dead man sends you a warning.”

“I can, and I did.”

“What are you going to do?”

“Check the lamp. Check the bell. Check everything.”

“I’ll help.”

“No.”

“I’m almost eighteen.”

“You’re sixteen.”

“Closer to eighteen than I used to be.”

“Go home, Tom.”

He opened his mouth to argue, then saw her face and thought better of it. At the stairs, he paused.

“My mother says the dead only send letters when the living have ignored every other warning.”

“Your mother also says nutmeg cures baldness.”

“She might be right. You never see bald nutmegs.”

Despite herself, Mara smiled.

Tom vanished down the stairs.

By noon, the fog had swallowed Bellweather.

From the lighthouse gallery, Mara could usually see the entire island: the crooked row of houses along Harbor Lane, the chapel steeple, the fields divided by stone walls, and the harbor where red and yellow boats nodded at their ropes. Now she saw only a white wall.

The lamp continued to burn.

She inspected the oil reservoir, polished the reflectors, tested the gears, and cleaned the wick. Everything was in order. Then she climbed to the bell chamber.

The lighthouse bell hung in the western tower, green with age. It had been cast on the mainland a hundred and twelve years before, after three ships vanished in a single foggy week. Along its rim ran the words:

WHAT THE LIGHT CANNOT GUIDE, THE BELL SHALL WARN.

Mara pulled the rope.

Nothing happened.

She pulled again.

The rope moved loosely through her hands.

Mara climbed onto the wooden platform and examined the mechanism. The iron chain connecting the rope to the clapper had been cut.

Not broken.

Cut.

The links bore fresh silver scars.

Below, the clock began to ring.

One.

Two.

Three.

It continued until thirteen.

As the final note trembled into silence, someone knocked on the lighthouse door.

Mara descended slowly, carrying her father’s old boat hook.

The knocking came again.

Three measured taps.

She opened the door.

A man stood in the fog.

He was tall and broad-shouldered, wearing a black coat that streamed with water. His face was pale, his beard full of gray. On his left hand he wore one woolen glove.

The right hand was bare.

“Mara,” he said.

Her grip tightened around the boat hook.

The man smiled, and the years fell away from his face.

It was her father’s smile.

“No,” Mara whispered.

“I’ve come home.”

She slammed the door.

The man caught it with his bare hand. His fingers curled around the edge.

“Mara, wait.”

“My father is dead.”

“I was lost.”

“For seven years?”

“The sea is larger than you think.”

She pushed hard against the door, but he was stronger.

Then the lighthouse lamp went out.

Darkness dropped through the tower.

The man outside stopped pushing.

From somewhere in the fog came the sound of water running over stones. Underneath it, barely audible, hundreds of voices began whispering Mara’s name.

She remembered the letter.

Do not trust what returns with the fog.

Mara drove the boat hook through the gap. The iron point struck the man’s shoulder.

He cried out—not in pain, but anger.

For an instant, his face changed. His eyes became black hollows, his mouth a wide, dripping crack. Seaweed hung from his teeth.

Mara shoved the door closed and dropped the bar into place.

Something struck the other side hard enough to shake dust from the ceiling.

Then came her father’s voice.

“Please, little tern.”

Mara froze.

He had called her that when she was a child because she had followed him everywhere, skipping across the rocks while he repaired storm lamps and painted harbor posts.

“Please,” the voice repeated. “It’s cold.”

Mara backed away from the door.

The whispering outside grew louder.

She climbed the stairs in darkness. By touch, she found the emergency lantern and lit it. Its small flame revealed the lamp chamber: the great central lens, the oil pipes, the brass tools hanging neatly on hooks.

The main wick was wet.

Mara touched it, then smelled her fingers.

Salt water.

Impossible. The reservoir was sealed.

Below, glass shattered.

They were coming through the ground-floor windows.

Mara pulled the wick free and replaced it. She drained the reservoir, refilled it with fresh oil, and struck a match.

The wick caught.

The flame rose blue, then gold.

As the lens began to turn, a beam cut through the fog. For half a second, Mara saw shapes crowded around the lighthouse.

Sailors in torn uniforms.

Fishermen with shells growing from their eyes.

Children dripping black water.

And her father standing among them with the boat hook buried in his shoulder.

The beam passed, and the fog closed again.

The lighthouse door cracked below.

Mara ran to the bell chamber. The cut chain could not be repaired in time, but the clapper itself was still intact—a thick iron tongue suspended inside the bell.

She looked at the clock.

Its hands spun wildly.

The note had said to ring the bell before midnight. But the clock was useless, and the fog hid the sky.

From below came the splintering of wood.

Mara searched the chamber. There were tools, spare gears, coils of wire, and a heavy hammer. She struck the bell with the hammer.

A dull clang rolled through the tower.

Outside, the whispering stopped.

Then the dead screamed.

The sound struck the lighthouse like a wave. Windows rattled. The lamp flame bent almost flat.

Mara hit the bell again.

The hammer bounced from the metal, numbing her arm. The second note was louder. In the lantern room below, something shrieked.

She lifted the hammer a third time.

A hand seized her wrist.

Mara spun.

Her father stood behind her.

His black coat dripped onto the floor. The wound in his shoulder had closed around the boat hook’s iron point, which still protruded from his body.

“You always were stubborn,” he said.

She tried to pull free.

His hand was ice.

“You’re not him.”

“Some of me is.”

The bell chamber seemed to fill with the smell of storms: salt, wet rope, lightning-burned air.

“What are you?”

His expression softened. “A door left open too long.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No.” He glanced toward the bell. “But we have little time.”

Mara stopped struggling.

Below them, the other dead moved through the lighthouse. Their wet footsteps sounded on the stairs.

“You sent the letter,” she said.

“I wrote it seven years ago.”

“Before you died?”

“Before I went outside.”

“You knew?”

“I suspected.”

The thing wearing her father’s face released her wrist.

Mara stepped back, keeping the hammer raised.

Elias—or what remained of him—looked toward the fog. “The night I disappeared, the sea was full of voices. They called from the rocks. They knew the names of everyone on Bellweather. The lamp went out because they wished it to.”

“And tonight?”

“They have grown stronger.”

“Why?”

“Because the islanders stopped ringing the bell.”

Mara frowned. “We ring it for storms.”

“You ring the foghorn for storms. The bell has not been rung properly since I died.”

“What does properly mean?”

“Twelve times before midnight on the first winter fog.”

“That isn’t written anywhere.”

“It was passed from keeper to keeper. I thought I would have time to tell you.”

Anger rose through Mara, hot and sudden. “You thought? You left me alone in a storm. You climbed onto the gallery and never came back. Then seven years later, you arrive with a riddle in a bottle?”

“I was trying to save you.”

“You should have trusted me.”

“You were fifteen.”

“I was old enough to hold the rope.”

“And I was frightened it would pull you over with me.”

They stared at one another.

His face was the face she remembered, but not exactly. The sea had smoothed something from it. His warmth, perhaps. Or his certainty.

The dead had reached the stairs below the bell chamber.

Elias looked down.

“You must ring twelve times.”

“I’ve struck it twice.”

“No. The first was a test. The bell answers only when the living ring for the dead.”

“I don’t know what that means.”

“You will.”

The first drowned sailor appeared at the top of the stairs.

His blue coat belonged to another century. A crab moved beneath the skin of his cheek. Behind him climbed a woman in a torn wedding dress, and behind her came dozens more.

Elias stepped between them and Mara.

“Go,” he said.

“Where?”

“The lamp.”

“They’re coming from the stairs.”

“Use the clock shaft.”

Mara looked toward the narrow maintenance hatch in the wall.

“I’m not leaving you.”

A sad smile crossed his face. “You already did.”

The drowned sailor lunged.

Elias caught him, and they crashed against the railing. The bell chamber filled with grasping hands and streaming water.

Mara crawled through the maintenance hatch.

The shaft beyond was scarcely wider than her shoulders. Clock weights hung in the darkness, each large enough to crush her. She climbed down the iron rungs until she reached the mechanism room behind the clock face.

Moonlight should have shone through the glass numerals. Instead, pale fog pressed against them like a blind eye.

The gears turned at impossible speed.

Mara stepped between them, ducking under spinning rods and swinging levers. On the central axle, she saw a coil of rope.

Bell rope.

Her father had rigged a second line through the clock mechanism.

She understood at once. When the clock reached midnight, the gears would pull the bell clapper. But the clock had failed long ago, and someone—or something—had cut the main chain to prevent the bell from being rung by hand.

Mara grabbed the loose rope.

It ran upward through the ceiling.

If she tied it to the clock’s striking arm, the mechanism could ring the bell. But the hands spun too quickly to measure time, and the gear teeth were slick with salt.

Behind her, the clock face cracked.

A wet hand pushed through the glass.

Mara threaded the rope around the striking arm. The mechanism jerked, nearly taking her fingers with it. She tied a knot, pulled it tight, and leaped aside.

The arm descended.

Above, the bell rang.

One.

The cracked clock face burst inward.

Drowned hands reached through, tearing away brass and glass. Mara backed toward the shaft.

The arm rose and fell.

Two.

The fog outside recoiled. Through the broken clock face, Mara saw the island below.

Lights shone in every house. People stood at their windows, watching figures gather in the streets.

Three.

The dead turned toward the lighthouse.

Four.

The drowned crawled through the clock face.

Mara kicked one back. It fell without a sound, vanishing into fog before it reached the rocks.

Five.

The rope strained.

One of the gears shifted. The knot began sliding toward the end of the striking arm.

Mara grabbed it.

The mechanism lifted her from the floor.

Six.

She swung over the spinning gears. Metal teeth tore the hem of her coat.

Seven.

A drowned child climbed through the window. He looked no older than five. Water poured from his mouth when he spoke.

“Help me.”

Mara knew that if she looked closely, he would become someone she had lost.

She shut her eyes.

Eight.

The rope slipped another inch.

She wrapped it around her wrist.

Nine.

Pain shot through her shoulder as the arm rose.

Somewhere above, the dead screamed and the bell chamber shook.

Ten.

A figure seized Mara’s ankle.

She opened her eyes.

Tom Tern clung to her boot.

His face was white, his hair dripping.

“Mara,” he pleaded. “Don’t let me fall.”

For one terrible instant, she believed him.

Then she remembered his foolish jokes, his bright red scarf, the flour always dusting his sleeves.

This Tom wore no scarf.

And his hands were swollen from the sea.

Mara kicked him in the face.

The thing fell backward into the gears.

Its body twisted like rope, bones cracking as the mechanism pulled it between two brass wheels. Black water sprayed across the room.

Eleven.

The striking arm rose for the final time.

The rope knot unraveled.

Mara caught the loose end with both hands, but the force dragged her toward the gears. Her boots slipped on the flooded floor.

She thought of her father outside in the storm, holding the rail with one gloved hand.

She thought of seven years of anger.

Seven years of keeping the lamp lit.

The rope slid through her bleeding palms.

Then another pair of hands closed over hers.

Elias stood behind her.

His coat was torn. One side of his face had collapsed into shadow. Yet his grip was strong.

“Together,” he said.

They pulled.

The striking arm descended.

Twelve.

The bell’s final note was not loud.

It was vast.

It moved through stone, through sea, through every bone in Mara’s body. The fog folded inward as if drawn into a great breath. The drowned figures froze.

Then they began to vanish.

Not violently. Not with screams.

They faded like reflections after a stone breaks water.

The sailors disappeared first, then the fishermen, then the women and children. Some looked relieved. Others looked afraid. The false Tom was gone before Mara could see his face change.

Elias remained.

Dawn shone through the broken clock face.

He released the rope.

Mara turned to him. “Why are you still here?”

“You haven’t let me go.”

Her throat tightened. “That seems unfair.”

“The sea often is.”

“Will I see you again?”

“I hope not here.”

She looked at his bare right hand.

“I kept your glove,” she said.

“I know.”

“Do you remember where you lost the other one?”

He smiled. “You dropped it in the harbor when you were eight. Then you lied and said a gull stole it.”

A laugh escaped her, half sob.

“You knew?”

“Of course.”

The dawn passed through him now. She could see the gears behind his coat.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“So am I.”

“For what?”

“For spending so long being angry.”

“You had every right.”

“I know. But I’m tired of it.”

Elias nodded as if she had completed a difficult lesson.

Then he reached out and touched two cold fingers to her forehead.

“Goodbye, little tern.”

“Goodbye, Father.”

He disappeared with the fog.

By sunrise, Bellweather Island was covered in broken windows, seawater, and dead fish. No one had died, though half the village claimed to have seen lost relatives standing outside their doors.

Tom Tern was found asleep in the bakery cellar with a rolling pin in one hand and a sack of nutmeg in the other.

When Mara returned to the lighthouse, she repaired the front door, replaced the shattered windows, and cleaned black water from the gears. It took three weeks.

She also fixed the clock.

On the first morning it showed the correct hour, the entire island gathered below to listen.

At noon, the lighthouse clock struck twelve.

Then, after a brief pause, the old warning bell rang once.

The islanders looked at Mara.

“Is it supposed to do that?” Tom called.

Mara stood on the gallery, one hand resting on the rail. The sea stretched clear and blue to the horizon. Near Widow’s Beach, a dark bottle rolled in the gentle surf, but she felt no need to retrieve it.

“No,” she said.

Then she smiled.

“But some clocks remember more than time.”
